checked: Checked singular they for generic and nonbinary singular reference, including ordinary they-verb agreement, against MLA Style Center and Chicago Manual of Style guidance: https://style.mla.org/using-singular-they/ and https://www.chicagomanualofstyle.org/qanda/data/faq/topics/Pronouns/faq0031.html.

Checked the lesson's claim that singular they has a long English history against the University of Illinois summary of OED evidence tracing it to 1375: https://blogs.uofi.uillinois.edu/view/25/677177.

Checked collective-noun agreement by unit versus individual members against Cambridge Grammar, which allows singular or plural agreement according to meaning: https://dictionary.cambridge.org/us/grammar/british-grammar/nouns-plural.

Checked Filipino personal-pronoun sets and ang/ng/sa-associated forms against KWF's Balarila and the University of Hawai‘i Filipino grammar tables; ako/ko/akin, siya/niya/kaniya, and sila/nila/kanila are supported: https://kwf.gov.ph/wp-content/uploads/Balarila-ng-Wikang-Pambansa-1.pdf and https://www.hawaii.edu/filipino/Grammar_Topics/Grammar_3-1.html.

Checked that Filipino siya is third-person singular without an English he/she gender split against University of Hawai‘i Press material glossing siya as he/she: https://manifold.uhpress.hawaii.edu/read/tagalog-for-beginners/section/5bb087e3-9a08-429e-b742-00c182e26f40.
Example #1: solving from the stem alone, Each is singular but can take gender-neutral singular their, so the answer is their.
Example #2: solving from the stem alone, company is treated as one organization, so the answer is its.
Example #3: solving from the stem alone, Liza and Carlo form a plural antecedent, so the answer is their.
Example #4: solving from the stem alone, she can refer to either Mrs. Santos or Anna; naming the intended person removes the ambiguity.
The lesson includes Core Concept, Examples, Speed Tricks & Shortcuts, and Traps to Watch For; the optional mnemonic section is omitted, and this pronoun lesson has no required figure.

The lesson serves the recorded goal by teaching English pronoun reference through number, meaning, singular they, collective and compound antecedents, mixed or/nor cases, and ambiguity, while limiting the Filipino note to introducing personal-pronoun forms.

findings.quote: Forms such as *his or her* are also possible in some contexts, but they are not inherently more grammatical than singular *their*. Do not assume an exam must prefer *his or her* unless the item or style guide explicitly establishes that convention.
findings.problem: This teaching prose uses abstract, advanced wording such as "inherently," "grammatical," and "explicitly establishes that convention," which is above the required Grade 5 reading level.

findings.quote: With antecedents joined by *or/nor*, a pronoun can become awkward if one option is singular and another plural. Instead of relying on a mechanical "nearest antecedent" rule for pronouns, rewrite for clarity when possible: "Neither the coach nor the players brought the equipment they needed" or "Neither the players nor the coach brought the required equipment."
findings.problem: Mixed singular/plural antecedents joined by or/nor are taught as a distinct exam-relevant case, but the Examples section has no worked example that makes the learner handle this case.

checked: Singular they states when it applies and distinguishes antecedent verb agreement from they-verb agreement; the lesson also notes that his or her may be used in some contexts.
Collective-noun reference states the unit-versus-members condition and notes English-variety differences, while compound and is qualified as normally plural.
Mixed or/nor reference states the singular/plural awkwardness condition and recommends rewriting for clarity instead of forcing a nearest-antecedent shortcut.
Ambiguous reference states the limiting condition directly: a pronoun should not leave two equally plausible antecedents.
